blocks.text: The most common applications of the principle to physical and chemical equilibria concern the effect of a change in concentration, the effect of a change in pressure, the effect of a change in temperature, and the effect of a catalyst on equilibrium; each is treated in topics 8.12 to 8.15.

blocks.alt: Four boxes: concentration changes in the bismuth chloride hydrolysis; pressure changes in ammonia synthesis; temperature changes in the exothermic SO3 and endothermic NO2 equilibria with their Kc values; and a small energy diagram with a red uncatalysed and a green catalysed hump between the same reactant and product levels. A summary box below separates the position of equilibrium from the equilibrium constant.
blocks.caption: Le Chatelier's principle applied to concentration, pressure, temperature and a catalyst (original diagram after topics 8.12 to 8.15 and Figure 8.3).
blocks.long_description: Adding a reactant or removing a product pushes the equilibrium right; adding a product or removing a reactant pushes it left. Raising the pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, so heating lowers Kc for the exothermic SO3 formation and raises it for the endothermic N2O4 dissociation. A catalyst lowers both activation barriers equally, reaching the same equilibrium sooner. Only temperature changes Kc itself.

blocks.prompt: Which single factor changes the value of the equilibrium constant, and what do the other factors change?
blocks.explanation: Only temperature changes Kc. Changes in concentration, pressure or volume move the position of equilibrium, the proportions of the mixture, while Kc stays the same; a catalyst changes neither the position nor Kc, only the speed of reaching equilibrium.

items: Four applications: concentration (8.12), pressure or volume (8.13), temperature (8.14), catalyst (8.15); only temperature changes Kc.
